question: Read data_description.txt. For every column with blanks, say whether a blank means 'feature absent', 'zero area' or 'truly unknown', and recommend a fill.
ai_answer: 27 of 79 columns have blanks. 15 mean the feature is absent (no pool, no alley, no basement), 9 are matching areas and counts that should be 0, LotFrontage and GarageYrBlt can be estimated, 1 (Electrical) is truly unknown.
challenge: Actuary: if PoolQC is blank because there is no pool, PoolArea should be 0 on those rows. Prove the reading, don't assert it.
test: Cross-checked each 'absent' column against its matching area or count column.
result: Every blank PoolQC row has PoolArea 0; the same holds for garage and basement blocks.
decision: Adopt the NA rules table; no mean imputation of absent features.
effect: Prevents the model inventing pools and garages; rules shown in Exhibit 2.3.

question: Can the test answers leak in from the public Ames data set? If so, external data is a disqualification risk.
ai_answer: First answer (wrong): yes. The test set looked like a re-split of the public 2,930 houses, so training on the public file would mean training on the answers.
challenge: AI's own check when trying to recover test prices for scoring: match the rows instead of assuming.
test: Matched all 1,465 training rows to the public file on 16 numeric columns; compared summary statistics.
result: 0 of 1,465 rows match; mean price $211k against $181k in the public file. The IAA data is synthetic, generated from Ames.
decision: Withdraw the leakage claim. Whether external data is allowed becomes a rules question for hour one.
effect: A wrong claim found and corrected by testing it. The playbook was amended.

question: Look at how the first-prize winner solved it. Can you reproduce his work? If I use you to design this, can you produce the same kind of results?
ai_answer: Read his notebook in full, rebuilt his environment (including his R package midr), and reran his code with his settings.
challenge: Reproduce before improving: a challenger is only meaningful against a verified incumbent.
test: Compare each component score to the figures printed in his notebook.
result: LightGBM and CatBoost match to six decimals; ensemble 0.0934 against his reported 0.0932 (newer XGBoost).
decision: Treat his rerun as the 'current model' in the filing.
effect: Every later comparison is like for like: same houses, same folds, same exclusions.

question: Where can the incumbent be beaten without tuning harder?
ai_answer: All three of its models are boosted trees, so their errors are highly correlated and averaging them gains little. Add a family whose errors differ: penalised linear models (a GLM with shrinkage) and kernel models.
challenge: Actuary: show it is not luck of one split.
test: Eight models, three different fold splits, paired bootstrap on the same houses.
result: Error 0.0882 against 0.0925 (4.7% lower); the 95% interval of the gain excludes zero on all three splits. Lasso alone edges the incumbent.
effect: The accuracy gain came from method choice, not from tuning (a 30-trial search did not beat hand-set settings).

question: Rate filings for our Canadian P&C lines have to justify every algorithm choice in a set structure. Adapt that structure to document this model, and tell me what you need from me as judgment.
ai_answer: Reorganised the work into filing sections mapped to FSRA guidance and the NAIC predictive-model checklist, each opening with what a reviewer would ask. Added a judgment register: eight decisions, four that only the actuary can make.
challenge: Actuary: where the technical terms are, give an example of how to read them simply.
test: Every exhibit given a 'How to read this' note with a worked example (for instance RMSLE 0.089 is about ±$27k on a $300k house).
result: A model document a regulator, a judge or a non-actuary can follow.
decision: Use the filing structure inside the notebook sections.
effect: Interpretability and documentation criteria (40% of the 2025 score) addressed by design.

question: Looking at the double-lift chart, my natural question is overfitting. Did we fit a model that gets every point right? How did we preserve predictive power? Is that addressed anywhere?
ai_answer: Partly: every score was already out of fold, but the document never said so and nothing was tested on data never touched.
challenge: Lock away 20% of houses before any fitting, weighting or selection; rerun both pipelines end to end; score once.
test: Apparent error (fitted houses) against cross-validated against locked hold-out, for both models; paired bootstrap on the hold-out.
result: Both models look about twice as accurate on fitted houses (0.04 to 0.05) as on unseen ones (about 0.09). Hold-out: 0.0867 against 0.0900, same direction, but the 293-house interval just includes zero.
decision: Report the weaker, honest hold-out claim; rest significance on the larger cross-validated tests.
effect: Two new exhibits and a controls table; the summary claim was made more cautious, not stronger.

question: Which inputs would not exist at the moment the model is used?
ai_answer: Month and year of sale, sale type and sale condition are only known after a house sells. An underwriter checking insured value could not supply them.
challenge: Quantify the cost before recommending removal.
test: Refit the two strongest models with and without the four variables on the same folds.
decision: Recommend dropping them for any pre-sale use (judgment J2).
effect: Keeps the model usable for the stated business purpose.

question: Which predictions move most against the current model, and why?
ai_answer: Two Edwards houses move by +165% and +250%. They resemble the two training sales excluded as non-market; the current model prices them with a separate line, my build applies no treatment.
challenge: This is a gap in the AI's own build, not an improvement. Record it as a decision, do not hide it.
test: Impact analysis across all 1,465 test houses.
result: 90% of houses move by 5% or less; 4 move by more than 15%.
decision: Judgment J3 opened for the actuary: refer such houses to an underwriter, or apply a segment model.
effect: The AI surfaced a weakness in its own work for a human decision.

question: You did not build this notebook. Score it against the five judging criteria, then try to break the model: find a leak, an overfit, a claim the evidence does not support.
ai_answer: To be run in a fresh session on the final notebook.
effect: Peer review by a reviewer that did not build the model, as the actuarial standards expect.
